subject: Physics
topic: Current Electricity — Ohm's Law, Resistance, Circuits

questions.text: Ohm's Law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage across it. If the voltage is 12 V and the resistance is 4 Ω, the current is ____.
questions.explanation: I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A. Ohm's Law: V = IR. Common errors: multiplying instead of dividing (12×4=48), or inverting incorrectly (4/12).

questions.text: The SI unit of electrical resistance is the Ohm (Ω), named after Georg Ohm. One Ohm is defined as ____.
questions.explanation: From Ohm's Law: R = V/I. So 1 Ω = 1 V/A (one volt per ampere). Option B is conductance (Siemens, S = A/V). Option D defines 1 Volt (J/C), not Ohm.

questions.text: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance of the combination?
questions.explanation: Parallel: 1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 3/6 + 2/6 + 1/6 = 6/6 = 1. So R = 1 Ω. In parallel, total resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance (less than 2 Ω). Option B (11 Ω) is the series sum — a common error.

questions.text: Resistivity (ρ) of a conductor depends on ____.

options.option_text: Material of the conductor and its temperature only
Length, cross-section, material, and temperature combined
Cross-sectional area and length of the conductor only
Only temperature, regardless of material composition

questions.explanation: Resistivity (ρ) is an intrinsic material property that depends on: (1) the material itself and (2) temperature. It does NOT depend on the conductor's shape or size. Resistance (R = ρL/A) depends on length and cross-section, but resistivity does not. This is a classic exam trap: confusing resistance with resistivity.

questions.text: A 60 W bulb and a 100 W bulb are connected in series to a 220 V supply. Which bulb glows brighter?

options.option_text: 60 W bulb — higher resistance in series means more voltage drop
100 W bulb — higher rated wattage always means more brightness
Both glow equally — series connection equalises current only
Neither glows — series connection prevents current flow entirely

questions.explanation: Resistance of bulb = V²/P. 60 W bulb has R = 220²/60 ≈ 807 Ω; 100 W bulb has R = 220²/100 = 484 Ω. In series, same current flows, but P = I²R: higher resistance = more power dissipation. So the 60 W (higher resistance) bulb glows brighter in series — counterintuitively the lower-rated bulb wins.

questions.text: A household electric iron is rated 1000 W at 220 V. What is the current drawn by the iron during normal operation?
questions.explanation: P = V × I → I = P/V = 1000/220 = 4.545... ≈ 4.55 A. Resistance = V/I = 220/4.55 ≈ 48.4 Ω, or equivalently R = V²/P = 220²/1000 = 48,400/1000 = 48.4 Ω. The current drawn (~4.55 A) is why household circuits use 5 A fuses for such appliances.

questions.text: Two identical cells, each of EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are connected in series to a 2 Ω external resistor. What current flows through the circuit?
questions.explanation: Series cells: Total EMF = 1.5+1.5 = 3 V. Total internal resistance = 0.5+0.5 = 1 Ω. Total resistance = 1+2 = 3 Ω. I = EMF/Total R = 3/3 = 1.0 A. If cells were in parallel: EMF=1.5V, r=0.25Ω, I=1.5/2.25=0.67A. Series gives higher current when external resistance is larger than internal.
